interpreter: A program that reads and runs code step by step instead of compiling it first.
environment variable: A named system value that stores settings or paths programs can use.
IDE: A software application with tools for writing, testing, and organizing code in one place.
syntax: The set of rules that defines how code must be written and structured.
print: To send text or data from a program to the screen or another output.
indentation: Empty space at the start of a line used to organize code and show structure.
literal: A fixed value written directly in code, such as a number, text, or true/false.
variable: A named storage location that holds a value which can be read or changed.
data type: A category that tells what kind of value a piece of data represents.
type conversion: Changing a value from one data type to another, such as text to a number.
identifier: A name chosen by a programmer for things like variables, functions, or classes.
operator: A symbol that performs an action on values, such as addition or comparison.
f-string: A special string in Python that lets you insert values directly into text.
input: Data or values entered into a program, often from a keyboard or file.
boolean: A data type with only two possible values: true or false.
comparison operator: A symbol that compares two values and gives a true or false result.
condition: An expression that is true or false and controls whether code runs.
branch: A path in a program that runs only when a certain condition is met.
nested: Placed inside another structure of the same kind, such as a loop within a loop.
truthy: A value that evaluates as true in a boolean context, even if it is not literally true.
loop: A control structure that repeats a block of instructions multiple times automatically.
iteration: One single pass or repetition through a block of code in a loop.
range: An ordered sequence of numbers often used to control how many times a loop runs.
infinite loop: A loop that continues forever because its ending condition is never reached or satisfied.
break: A statement used to immediately exit the nearest enclosing loop before it would normally end.
continue: A statement that skips the rest of the current loop cycle and starts the next repetition.
function: A named, reusable block of code that performs a task and can take inputs and return output.
parameter: A named variable listed in a function definition that receives a value passed into the function.
argument: The actual value supplied to a function when it is called, assigned to a parameter.
return value: The result a function sends back to the code that called it after finishing its task.
scope: The part of a program where a particular variable or name can be accessed and used.
docstring: A string placed in code to document what a function, module, or class does.
list: A mutable ordered collection that can hold multiple items, typically using square brackets.
index: A number indicating the position of an item in a sequence, often starting from zero.
tuple: An immutable ordered collection of values, usually written with parentheses and commas.
slice: A selected portion of a sequence defined by start, stop, and optional step positions.
set: An unordered programming collection storing only unique, non-duplicate data values.
dictionary: A key-value paired data structure that maps unique keys to associated stored values.
mutable: Describes data values that can be modified directly after their initial creation in code.
multiple return values: A function feature that lets a single function return more than one output result at once.
default parameter: A pre-set function argument value used when no custom value is passed during a function call.
keyword argument: A function argument identified by an explicit parameter name instead of its call position.
variable-length argument: A flexible function parameter that accepts an unspecified number of passed input values.
lambda: A small anonymous inline function that typically contains only a single short expression.
higher-order function: A function that takes other functions as inputs or returns a function as its output.
closure: A nested function that remembers and retains values from its surrounding outer function scope.
encoding: The process of converting text or data into a specific byte format for storage or transmission.
file object: A programming interface that lets code interact with and manipulate an opened external file.
with statement: A control structure that automatically handles resource setup and cleanup for safe operations.
mode: A setting that defines which operations, like reading or writing, are allowed on an opened file.
read / write: Core file operations that respectively access existing file data or save new data to the file.
append: A write operation that adds new data to the end of an existing file without overwriting it.
exception: An unexpected runtime error event that disrupts a program's normal ordered execution flow.
try-except: A code structure used to catch and handle raised exceptions without crashing the whole program.
finally: A code block that runs after a try-catch block, whether an error occurred or not.
module: A single file containing related code that can be imported and reused in other programs.
package: A collection of related modules organized in a directory for easy reuse and distribution.
third-party library: Prebuilt code made by someone outside the original platform, added to projects to add features.
JSON: A lightweight text format using key-value pairs to store and exchange data between systems.
serialization: The process of converting an in-memory object into a storable or transmittable format.
visualization: A visual representation of data, such as a chart or graph, made to reveal patterns.
line chart: A chart that connects data points with lines, commonly used to show changes over time.
axis: A reference line on a chart, usually horizontal or vertical, used to measure data values.
legend: A chart key that explains the meaning of colors, symbols, or line styles used in it.
map chart: A chart that displays data tied to geographic areas or locations on a map.
GeoJSON: A JSON-based format used to encode geographic data such as points, lines, and regions.
region: A defined geographic area, such as a country, province, or city, used in data analysis.
heatmap: A chart using color intensity to show values or frequency across areas or categories.
coordinate: A set of numbers, often latitude and longitude, that identifies a point on Earth or a chart.
province: A major administrative division within a country, often similar to a state.
bar chart: A chart that uses rectangular bars of varying lengths to compare values across categories.
timeline: A visual sequence arranged by time, used to show events or data in chronological order.
animation: Creating moving images by showing a sequence of still pictures over time.
dataset: A structured collection of related data, often stored as records or files.
render: To generate a visible image or output from digital content or code.
summary: A brief statement that presents the main points of larger information.
class: A blueprint for creating objects, defining their properties and behaviors.
object: A self-contained unit in code that combines data and behavior.
instance: A specific object created from a class with its own values.
encapsulation: Keeping an object's data and methods together while hiding internal details.
inheritance: A mechanism where one class receives properties and behaviors from another.
polymorphism: Treating different classes through a shared interface so methods behave appropriately.
RDD: An immutable distributed collection of data records processed in parallel across a cluster.
big data: Extremely large and complex data collections that need special tools to process.
Spark: A fast distributed computing engine for processing large datasets in parallel.
distributed: Spread across multiple computers that work together as one system.
transformation: A data operation that creates a new distributed dataset from an existing one.
action: An operation that triggers computation and returns a result or writes output.
decorator: A function that modifies another function or class without changing its source code.
syntactic sugar: A convenient syntax feature that makes code easier to read without changing capability.
singleton: A design pattern that ensures a class has only one instance and provides a global access point.
factory pattern: A design pattern that uses special methods to create objects without specifying their exact concrete classes.
generator: A function or object that produces values one at a time and can pause between each result.
iterator: An object that traverses a collection one item at a time and keeps its current position.
process: An independent running program with its own memory space, system resources, and state.
thread: A lightweight execution path inside a process that shares memory and resources with other threads.
GIL: A lock in some Python interpreters that allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time.
lock: A synchronization tool that prevents multiple threads from accessing a shared resource at the same time.
thread pool: A managed group of reusable threads that performs many tasks efficiently without creating new threads repeatedly.
concurrency: The ability to manage multiple tasks at the same time by switching between them, possibly without true parallel execution.
socket: A programming endpoint for sending and receiving data across a network between two programs.
TCP: A reliable network protocol that establishes connections, orders data, and ensures packets arrive without errors.
HTTP: The protocol used by web browsers and servers to request and send hypertext resources over networks.
request: A message sent by a client to a server asking for data, an action, or a resource.
regular expression: A pattern language used to search, match, and replace text based on specific character rules.
metacharacter: A character in a pattern that has special meaning, such as controlling matches or repetition.
database: An organized collection of structured information or data, usually stored and accessed electronically.
table: A database structure that stores data in organized rows and columns, like a spreadsheet.
primary key: A column or set of columns that uniquely identifies each row in a database table.
query: A request for information or action written to retrieve or modify data in a database.
SQL: A standard language used to communicate with databases and create, read, update, or delete data.
foreign key: A field in one table that references the primary key of another table to link records.
attribute: A named property or characteristic of an object, table, or entity that stores a value.
method: A function defined inside a class that describes an action objects of that class can perform.
override: To define a method in a subclass that replaces a method with the same name in its parent class.
abstract class: A class that cannot be instantiated directly and provides a common base for subclasses to extend.
class attribute: A variable belonging to a class rather than an instance, shared by all objects created from that class.
static method: A method defined in a class that does not receive an instance or class as its first argument.
nonlocal: A keyword in Python used to declare that a variable refers to one in an enclosing function scope.
shallow copy: A copy that duplicates the outer object but shares references to the nested objects inside it.
deep copy: A copy that recursively duplicates the outer object and all nested objects, creating fully independent data.
port: A numbered endpoint used by network protocols to identify a specific process or service on a computer.
mutex: A locking mechanism that ensures only one thread can access a shared resource at a time.
yield: A keyword that pauses a function or generator and sends a value back to the caller while preserving state.
property: A special method in a class that lets you access or modify an attribute like a simple variable.
time complexity: A measure of how an algorithm's running time grows as the size of its input increases.
space complexity: A measure of how much memory an algorithm needs as its input size grows.
Big O notation: A way to describe an algorithm's worst-case time or resource growth using a standard notation.
linked list: A linear data structure where elements called nodes connect through pointers or references.
node: A basic unit in a data structure that stores data and may link to other nodes.
traversal: The process of visiting each element or node in a data structure exactly once.
bubble sort: A simple sorting algorithm that repeatedly compares neighboring items and swaps them if needed.
binary search: An efficient search that repeatedly divides a sorted list in half to locate a value.
binary tree: A tree data structure in which each node has at most two child nodes.
preorder traversal: A tree traversal method that visits a node before visiting its left and right subtrees.
quicksort: An efficient divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm that partitions data around a chosen pivot.
stability: A sorting property where equal elements keep their original relative order after sorting.
Linux: A free open-source operating system kernel used in many distributions and computing systems.
virtual machine: Software that emulates a physical computer and runs an operating system independently on one host.
terminal: A text-based interface used to enter commands and interact with a computer system.
command: An instruction given to a computer, often typed, to perform a specific task.
permission: Settings that control which users can read, write, or execute files and resources.
path: A text location that specifies where a file or folder resides in a directory system.
DDL: A language subset used to define and modify database structures, such as tables and schemas.
DML: A category of SQL commands used to insert, read, update, and delete data in database tables.
constraint: A database rule that limits the values allowed in a table to keep data accurate and consistent.
inner join: A query operation that returns only rows with matching values in both tables being joined.
subquery: A query nested inside another query, used to provide intermediate results for the outer query.
aggregate function: A function such as SUM or COUNT that calculates a single summary value from multiple rows.
GROUP BY: An SQL clause that groups rows sharing a value so aggregate functions can be applied per group.
pagination: A technique that divides a large set of query results into separate, numbered pages for display.
window function: A function that performs calculations across a related set of table rows without collapsing them into one row.
ndarray: A NumPy multi-dimensional array object that stores numbers of the same type in a grid shape.
shape: A tuple describing the size of an array along each dimension, such as rows and columns.
dimension: A direction or axis in an array, such as a row dimension or column dimension in tabular data.
broadcasting: A NumPy feature that lets arrays of different shapes be used together in arithmetic operations.
dtype: An attribute describing the type of data stored in an array, such as integer or float.
vectorization: Replacing slow Python loops with fast array operations applied to many values at once.
DataFrame: A pandas two-dimensional labeled data structure organized into rows and columns, like a spreadsheet table.
Series: A pandas one-dimensional labeled array that can hold a single column or sequence of values.
column: A vertical set of values in a table representing one attribute or field across all rows.
missing value: An absent or unknown data entry, often represented by null, NaN, or NA in a dataset.
slicing: Selecting a range or subset of elements from data using start and end positions.
groupby: Splitting data into groups by a category and calculating summary results for each group.
merge: Combining two related datasets by matching shared key columns into one table.
pivot table: A summary table that rearranges and aggregates data by categories for easier comparison.
apply: Using a function on each value, row, or column to transform data automatically.
sort values: Arranging data rows in ascending or descending order based on one or more columns.
duplicate: A data row or value that appears more than once in a dataset.
figure: The overall canvas or window that contains one or more data visualizations.
subplot: One of multiple charts placed inside a single figure for organized comparison.
histogram: A chart showing the distribution of numeric data with bars representing value ranges.
RFM: A customer analysis model using recency, frequency, and monetary value to rank buyers.
segmentation: Dividing customers or data into groups with similar traits or behavior.
boxplot: A chart displaying median, quartiles, range, and possible outliers in numeric data.
scatter plot: A graph showing relationships between two numeric variables using plotted points.
outlier: A data value unusually different from most other values and requiring review.
dashboard: A visual display of key charts and metrics used to monitor data at a glance.
programming: Creating instructions that tell a computer how to perform tasks and process data.
code: Written instructions in a programming language that computers execute to complete tasks.
chatbot: A computer program that understands and responds to written or spoken human conversation automatically.
prompt: A short instruction or question given to an AI or program to guide its response.
string: A sequence of letters, numbers, or symbols treated as text in programming.
execute: To run a command, script, or program so that a computer performs its instructions.
for loop: A control structure that repeats a block of code once for each item in a collection.
key: A unique name or identifier used to find an associated value in a data structure.
value: The actual data stored and accessed using a key in a dictionary or similar structure.
comparison: An operation that checks whether values are equal, greater, smaller, or related in another way.
file: A named collection of data or information saved on a computer or storage device.
read: To access and take in data from a file, input source, or user.
extract: To find and pull out specific information from text, data, or another source.
summarize: To briefly restate the main ideas or important details of a longer piece of information.
template: A reusable pattern or outline that provides a starting structure for documents or code.
reuse: To use the same code, data, or component again in different tasks or projects.
itinerary: A planned route or schedule showing travel dates, times, activities, and destinations.
library: A collection of prewritten code and functions that programmers can use to perform common tasks.
import: To bring code, functions, or data from another module or library into a current program.
install: To set up software or a library on a computer so it can be used.
pip: pip is a standard tool for installing and managing software packages for the Python programming language.
API: A set of standardized rules that allows different software applications to share data and functionality.
determinant: A determinant is a value calculated from a square matrix that shows its scaling factor and whether it has an inverse.
minor: For a matrix, the determinant of a square submatrix formed by removing one row and one column.
cofactor: A cofactor is a signed value found by deleting one row and column from a matrix and calculating the remaining determinant.
upper triangular: Describing a square matrix where every entry below the main diagonal has a value of zero.
Cramer rule: A theorem using determinants to solve square linear equation systems that have a single unique solution.
permutation: A permutation is an arrangement of items where the order of the items matters.
matrix: A matrix is a rectangular arrangement of numbers or symbols organized into rows and columns.
transpose: An operation that flips a matrix across its main diagonal, swapping corresponding row and column positions.
identity matrix: A square matrix with ones along its main diagonal and zeros in every other off-diagonal position.
inverse matrix: A square matrix that multiplies with its matching original matrix to produce the identity matrix.
adjugate: The transpose of a square matrix's cofactor matrix, commonly used to calculate the matrix inverse.
elementary transformation: A basic invertible operation applied to a matrix's rows or columns in linear algebra computations.
rank: The maximum count of linearly independent row or column vectors that exist within a given matrix.
block matrix: A matrix split into distinct smaller sub-matrices called blocks, treated as single entry units.
vector: An element of a vector space, typically represented as an ordered sequence of scalar numerical values.
linear combination: An expression formed by multiplying each vector in a set by a scalar then summing all resulting terms.
linearly dependent: A set of vectors is linearly dependent if one vector can be written as a combination of the others.
linearly independent: A set of vectors is linearly independent if no vector can be formed by combining the other vectors.
maximal independent set: An independent subset that becomes dependent whenever any remaining vector from the set is added.
rank of a vector set: The number of vectors in any maximal linearly independent subset of that vector set.
homogeneous system: A system of linear equations in which every constant term on the right side is zero.
non-homogeneous: Describing a linear system whose equations have at least one nonzero constant term.
general solution: A complete formula that describes every possible solution of a system of equations.
particular solution: Any single solution of a nonhomogeneous linear system, used with the homogeneous solution.
free variable: A variable that can be chosen freely when solving a system, determining other variables.
consistent: Having at least one solution; said of a system of equations that is not contradictory.
eigenvalue: A scalar λ such that a matrix times a nonzero vector equals λ times that vector.
eigenvector: A nonzero vector that stays on its own line when a matrix transforms it.
characteristic polynomial: The polynomial det(A − λI), whose roots are the eigenvalues of a square matrix A.
similar matrices: Two square matrices related by a change of basis, so B equals P inverse A P.
diagonalization: The process of finding a similar diagonal matrix for a given square matrix.
orthogonal matrix: A square matrix whose columns are unit vectors pairwise perpendicular, and whose inverse is its transpose.
quadratic form: A homogeneous polynomial of degree two, usually written x transpose A x for a symmetric matrix.
symmetric matrix: A square matrix that equals its transpose, with entries mirrored across its main diagonal.
standard form: A simplified canonical expression of a quadratic form under an invertible linear substitution.
congruent: Two symmetric matrices related by an invertible matrix and its transpose.
positive definite: A quadratic form or matrix whose value is positive for every nonzero vector.
inertia: The counts of positive, negative, and zero square terms in a quadratic form.
vector space: A set of vectors closed under addition and scalar multiplication, satisfying standard axioms.
subspace: A subset of a vector space that itself forms a vector space under the same operations.
basis: A linearly independent set of vectors whose linear combinations span the whole vector space.
coordinates: The scalar coefficients that express a given vector as a combination of basis vectors.
transition matrix: A matrix that converts coordinate representations of vectors from one basis to another.
limit: The value a function or sequence approaches as the input or index nears a point.
sequence: An ordered list of numbers or terms indexed by positive integers.
infinitesimal: A variable quantity whose absolute value becomes arbitrarily close to zero in a limit.
continuity: A property where a function has no breaks and its value equals its limiting value.
discontinuity: A point at which a function fails to be continuous, often through a gap or jump.
two important limits: Two foundational limits used to derive trigonometric and exponential derivative formulas.
derivative: The instantaneous rate of change of a function, found as the limit of a difference quotient.
differentiable: Having a well-defined derivative at a point or over an indicated domain.
chain rule: A rule for differentiating a composite function by multiplying the derivatives of its parts.
higher-order derivative: A derivative of a derivative, showing a rate of change beyond the first derivative.
differential: An infinitesimal change in a variable, used to express linear approximation and integration.
implicit differentiation: A method for finding derivatives when x and y are mixed together in an equation.
Rolle theorem: If a differentiable function has equal endpoint values, some interior point has zero derivative.
mean value theorem: A theorem stating that at some interior point the instantaneous rate equals the average rate.
Taylor formula: A formula expressing a function as a sum of terms based on its derivatives at a point.
L Hopital rule: A method for finding certain limits by differentiating numerator and denominator separately.
monotonicity: The property of always increasing or always decreasing over an interval.
extremum: A value or point where a function reaches a maximum or minimum.
inflection point: A point where a graph changes concavity, switching between concave up and concave down.
antiderivative: A function whose derivative equals a given function.
indefinite integral: The family of all antiderivatives of a function, including an added constant.
substitution: An integration method that replaces a complicated expression with a simpler variable.
integration by parts: A technique based on the product rule for integrating products of functions.
partial fraction: One of several simpler fractions obtained by splitting a rational function.
constant of integration: An arbitrary constant added to an antiderivative because constants differentiate to zero.
definite integral: A signed value representing net area between a curve and an interval on the x-axis.
Riemann sum: A finite sum estimating a definite integral using rectangular areas under a curve.
fundamental theorem: It links differentiation and integration, showing an integral can be reversed by a derivative.
improper integral: A definite integral with an infinite interval or an unbounded function at some point.
area between curves: The amount of plane region bounded by two curves, found by integrating their difference.
volume of revolution: The volume of a solid formed by rotating a plane region around a line.
partial derivative: The derivative of a multivariable function with respect to one variable while others are fixed.
total differential: A linear approximation of a function’s total change using changes in all its independent variables.
gradient: A vector of all partial derivatives, showing the direction and rate of fastest increase.
double integral: An integral of a function over a two-dimensional region in the plane.
iterated integral: A sequence of integrations performed one after another, each with respect to a different variable.
polar coordinates: A coordinate system using distance from a point and angle from a fixed direction.
partial sum: The sum of a finite number of terms from the beginning of an infinite series.
convergence: The property of a sequence or series approaching a finite limit as terms continue.
geometric series: A series where each term is the previous term multiplied by a constant ratio.
power series: An infinite series of terms with increasing powers of a variable and constant coefficients.
radius of convergence: The largest distance from the expansion center for which a power series remains convergent.
differential equation: An equation containing an unknown function and one or more of its derivatives.
order: The order of a differential equation is the highest derivative appearing in that equation.
separable equation: A differential equation that can be rearranged so each variable appears on a separate side.
initial value problem: A differential equation combined with a condition that specifies the unknown function's value at one point.
difference equation: An equation that relates successive values of a sequence using differences or earlier terms.
combination: A selection of items where order does not matter and each chosen item appears at most once.
factorial: The product of all positive integers up to a given number, shown by an exclamation mark.
addition principle: A counting rule stating that separate choices can be added when they are mutually exclusive.
multiplication principle: A counting rule stating that successive independent choices can be multiplied to count outcomes.
sample space: The set of all possible outcomes that can occur in a random experiment.
random experiment: A process with an unknown result that can be repeated, with several possible outcomes.
event: A set of one or more outcomes from a sample space to which a probability is assigned.
classical probability: A probability model where every outcome in a finite sample space is equally likely.
conditional probability: The probability that one event happens given that another event is already known to have happened.
Bayes formula: A formula that updates a probability using new evidence by relating conditional probabilities.
independence: A relationship between events where knowing one occurs does not change the probability of the other.
Bernoulli trial: A single random experiment with exactly two possible outcomes, often called success and failure.
random variable: A variable whose possible numerical values come from the outcomes of a random experiment.
distribution function: A function giving the probability that a random variable is less than or equal to a value.
probability density: A function describing relative likelihood for a continuous random variable near a possible value.
binomial distribution: The probability distribution of successful outcomes in a fixed number of independent Bernoulli trials.
Poisson distribution: probability model for the number of independent events occurring in a fixed interval or region
normal distribution: symmetric bell-shaped probability distribution in which values cluster around a central mean and extreme values are rare
uniform distribution: probability distribution in which all possible outcomes or intervals have equal likelihood over a defined range
joint distribution: probability distribution describing the simultaneous behavior of two or more random variables and their combined outcomes
marginal distribution: probability distribution of one random variable obtained by summing or integrating over the values of other variables
conditional distribution: probability distribution of one variable given known values or conditions involving one or more other variables
mutually independent: property of events or variables where the occurrence or value of one provides no information about the others
convolution: mathematical operation combining two probability distributions to produce the distribution of their sum
bivariate normal: joint probability distribution of two normally distributed variables whose relationship is described by means, variances, and correlation
mathematical expectation: long-run average value of a random variable, calculated as the weighted sum or integral over its possible values
variance: measure of spread equal to the average squared deviation of a random variable’s values from its mean
standard deviation: measure of spread equal to the square root of variance, expressed in the same units as the data
covariance: measure of how much two random variables change together, indicating the direction of their linear relationship
correlation coefficient: standardized measure of the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two variables, ranging from minus one to one
moment: expected value of a power of a random variable, used to describe properties such as mean, variance, and skewness
Chebyshev inequality: theorem stating that a random variable is unlikely to lie far from its mean, with a bound based on variance
law of large numbers: principle that sample averages approach the expected value as the number of independent trials grows large
central limit theorem: result that sums or averages of many independent random variables tend toward a normal distribution
convergence in probability: A sequence of random variables becomes increasingly likely to stay close to a fixed target value as sample size grows.
independent identically distributed: Random variables have the same probability distribution and are statistically unrelated to one another.
standardize: Transform data by subtracting its mean and dividing by its standard deviation, usually to unit scale.
population: The complete collection of individuals, items, or outcomes about which statistical conclusions are sought.
sample: A subset of a population selected or observed to provide information about the whole group.
statistic: A number calculated from sample data, often used to estimate a population parameter or test a claim.
sample mean: The arithmetic average of observed sample values, obtained by summing them and dividing by sample size.
sample variance: A measure describing how far sample values lie from their average, using squared deviations and n minus one.
chi-square distribution: A right-skewed probability distribution formed by summing squares of independent standard normal variables.
t distribution: A symmetric bell-shaped probability distribution used for estimating means when population variance is unknown.
point estimation: Using sample data to calculate a single numerical estimate of an unknown population parameter.
method of moments: An estimation method that matches sample moments, such as averages, to corresponding theoretical population moments.
maximum likelihood: A method choosing parameter values that make the observed sample data most probable under the assumed model.
unbiased: Having an expected value equal to the true population parameter, so estimates do not systematically overestimate or underestimate.
consistency: Property of an estimator converging toward the true parameter value as the sample size becomes sufficiently large.
confidence interval: A range of values, constructed from sample data, designed to contain an unknown parameter with a specified confidence level.
hypothesis testing: A statistical procedure that uses sample evidence to decide whether to reject or retain a statement about a population.
null hypothesis: A default statement of no effect or no difference, tested against an alternative in statistical hypothesis testing.
significance level: The probability of rejecting a true null hypothesis, set before a statistical test.
Type I error: A false positive result where a true null hypothesis is incorrectly rejected.
p value: The probability of observing data at least as extreme as the sample result if the null hypothesis were true.
rejection region: The range of test values for which the null hypothesis is rejected.
